returns.say: Alright, here's the idea. Every return measure answers how much did I make, but each one makes a different assumption about time and reinvestment, and the exam tests whether you know which. A simple rate is total return divided by years held, with no compounding, so it ignores the time value of money. A compound rate assumes interest and principal get reinvested, and you solve it with the TVM or IRR keys. Holding period return is the whole-period gain, including income, over the starting value, but it has no time element, so it overstates the annual figure if held more than a year and understates it if held less. Total return is income plus appreciation, and SEC yield is a standardized thirty-day fund yield, income only. Walk Dana: she earned forty-five percent total over six years. Her simple rate is forty-five over six, seven and a half percent. Her compound rate, with PV of minus one, FV of one point four five and N of six, is about six point three nine percent, lower because growth compounds. Now Luis: he bought a bond for nine sixty, collected one forty of interest, and sold for ten ten. His HPR is one ninety over nine sixty, about nineteen point eight percent, but we don't know whether he held it one year or five. The exam trap: you can't compare HPRs across investments until you know the holding period, and a multi-year HPR always looks bigger than the true annual return. To a client: your statement shows nearly twenty percent since you bought, but that covers several years, so let's look at the annual figure before comparing it with anything.

Alright, two ways to average returns. The arithmetic mean is the plain average of the periodic returns, no compounding, no reinvestment. The geometric mean is the constant compound rate that turns a dollar into the actual ending value, and it's the preferred way to state a security's historical return. To get it, multiply one plus each return together, take the nth root, and subtract one. Walk four years of fund returns: plus ten, minus five, plus eighteen, plus seven. The arithmetic mean is thirty over four, seven and a half percent. Now multiply: one point one zero times point nine five times one point one eight times one point zero seven gives about one point three one nine four. Plug it in with N of four and the geometric mean is about seven point one eight percent. Here's the one that makes it click. Up twenty percent, then down twenty percent. The arithmetic mean is zero. The geometric mean is about minus two percent, and that's the truth, you actually lost money. The exam trap: the geometric mean is always below the arithmetic mean unless every period's return is identical, in which case they're equal. So any answer showing a geometric mean above the arithmetic mean is wrong on sight. To a client: an average of seven and a half percent sounds good, but what your money actually compounded at was about seven point two, and the compound number is the one to plan with.

Alright, this pair trips people up, so here's the clean split. A time-weighted return ignores the investor's later buys and sells. It measures the investment, or the manager, and it's what most published mutual fund returns use. A dollar-weighted return includes every dollar in and out, and it measures the investor's own experience, it's really an IRR on the client's cash flows. Walk Omar. He buys one share at forty. At the end of year one he gets a two dollar dividend and buys a second share at forty-six. At the end of year two he sells both at fifty-two. For the time-weighted return, follow one share: minus forty, plus two, plus fifty-two, and the IRR is about sixteen and a half percent. For the dollar-weighted return, use Omar's actual dollars: minus forty, then two minus forty-six, which is minus forty-four, then two shares at fifty-two, one hundred four. That IRR is about fifteen point four percent. Omar earned less than the stock because he put more money in just before a weaker year. The exam trap: when cash flows are quarterly, the textbook annualizes the periodic IRR by multiplying by four, not by compounding. Compounding gives a different number that isn't the book's answer. To a client: the fund's published number tells you how the manager did, but yours also reflects when you added or pulled money, so if you invested more right before a dip, you'll trail the fund even though you own the same thing.

Alright, here's how inflation, taxes and compounding change the number. The nominal rate is the stated rate before inflation, for a bond that's its coupon. The real rate is inflation-adjusted, and you use the exact formula, not subtraction: one plus nominal, divided by one plus inflation, minus one. After-tax return is the nominal rate times one minus the marginal rate. After-tax real return takes that after-tax figure and runs it through the same division. Walk Priya's seven percent bond, with two and a half percent inflation and a thirty percent combined tax rate. Real pre-tax: one point zero seven over one point zero two five, minus one, is about four point three nine percent. The shortcut, seven minus two and a half, gives four and a half, close but not exact. After-tax: seven times point seven is four point nine percent. After-tax real: one point zero four nine over one point zero two five, minus one, is about two point three four percent. Now APR versus EAR. APR is the periodic rate times the periods per year, no compounding. EAR is the true annual rate once compounding inside the year counts. A card at one and a half percent a month has an APR of eighteen percent, but an EAR of about nineteen and a half. The exam trap: the exam wants the division formula for real return, and over long projections like retirement needs, the subtraction shortcut creates sizable dollar errors. To a client: your bond pays seven percent, but after taxes and inflation you're really growing your buying power about two point three percent a year, and that's the number that matters for your retirement plan.

Alright, three risk-adjusted measures, and the key is which risk each one uses. Jensen's alpha is the portfolio return minus the CAPM required return, which is the risk-free rate plus beta times the market's excess return. It uses beta, it's an absolute measure, and positive alpha means you beat the required return and plot above the security market line. Treynor is excess return over the risk-free rate, divided by beta. Sharpe is excess return divided by standard deviation, total risk. Treynor and Sharpe are relative measures, so a lone number means nothing, you compare it with another fund or the benchmark, and higher is better. Jensen and Treynor need an R squared of at least point seven; Sharpe works almost always. Walk one portfolio: return eleven percent, beta one point two, standard deviation sixteen, market nine, risk-free three, R squared point eight five. CAPM required is three plus one point two times six, ten point two percent, so alpha is plus point eight. Treynor is eight over one point two, about six point six seven. Sharpe is eight over sixteen, point five. The exam trap: an undiversified fund can look great on Treynor and Jensen, which only see beta, and poor on Sharpe, which sees total risk. If R squared is below point seven, ignore the beta-based answers and pick by Sharpe. To a client: this manager beat the market by two percent but took on more risk to do it, and after adjusting for that risk he added about point eight percent, which is still positive, and that's what we want to see.

Alright, the information ratio grades an active manager. It asks how much extra return was earned per unit of extra risk taken by straying from the benchmark. The formula is portfolio return minus benchmark return, divided by the standard deviation of that excess return, which is called tracking error or active risk. A ratio of point five or higher often marks a top-quartile manager in its asset class. If the benchmark is the risk-free rate, the information ratio reduces to the Sharpe ratio. Walk two managers against an eight percent benchmark. Fund Q returned nine and a half with three percent tracking error, so one and a half over three, point five. Fund R returned ten with six percent tracking error, so two over six, about point three three. Pick Q: less return, but far more efficient per unit of active risk. Now choosing the right measure. If R squared is around point four five, below point seven, Sharpe only. Fund K at ten percent with a twelve percent standard deviation scores about point five eight, fund L at thirteen with twenty scores point five, so K wins even though Treynor would favor L. If you see tracking error or active risk, think information ratio. The exam trap: compare Sharpe ratios only within one asset class, because recent winners cluster at the top, and ranking across classes would throw out an entire lagging class like emerging markets. To a client: both managers beat the index, but one took twice the off-benchmark risk to get a bit more, and I'd rather pay for the one who's more efficient.

Alright, indices and benchmarks. The Dow is price-weighted, thirty stocks, the sum of prices divided by a divisor that's now below one. That means a ninety dollar stock moves it three times as much as a thirty dollar stock. It ignores cash dividends and shares outstanding, yet still correlates above point nine five with the S and P five hundred. Cap-weighted indices, like the S and P five hundred, weight each firm by its value relative to the whole index, so a forty-five billion dollar company in a three hundred billion dollar index drives fifteen percent of its moves. Match the benchmark to the asset class: S and P five hundred for U.S. large cap, S and P MidCap four hundred for mid cap, Russell two thousand for small cap, and MSCI EAFE for developed international, which leaves out the U.S. and Canada. A client holds fifty percent large cap, thirty percent small cap and twenty percent international, and earned seven point nine percent. The indices returned ten, six and four. Weight them: five plus one point eight plus point eight, a blend of seven point six. The portfolio beat its true benchmark, even though it trailed the S and P. The exam trap: a small-cap fund is judged against a small-cap index, not the S and P. To a client: the S and P was up ten percent, but only half your money is in big U.S. companies, and against a yardstick built the way you're actually invested, you came out ahead.

returns.at: Bond yields: current yield, YTM, YTC
returns.say: Alright, bond yields. First the calculator defaults, unless told otherwise: future value is plus one thousand face, payment is the annual coupon divided by two, N is years times two, and price is a negative present value. Current yield is the annual coupon divided by the current market price. Yield to maturity is the bond's IRR if held to maturity, and it assumes coupons get reinvested at that same yield. Yield to call is the same calculation, but the future value is the call price and N is the periods to first call. Walk Bond A, a discount bond: eight years, five percent coupon, price nine forty. Current yield is about five point three two percent, and YTM, with sixteen periods and a twenty-five dollar payment, is about five point nine five. Bond B: ten years, seven percent coupon, price ten eighty, callable in four years at ten twenty. Current yield is about six point four eight, YTM about five point nine three, and YTC about five point two one. Now the ordering. For a discount bond, coupon is below current yield, below YTM, below YTC. For a premium bond, it flips, coupon is above current yield, above YTM, above YTC. The logic: a discount bond's gain to par arrives sooner if called, a premium bond's loss arrives sooner. The exam trap: if the coupon is paid annually, switch to one payment per year, full annual coupon, and N equals years. To a client: this bond shows a nice yield to maturity, but it's priced above face and can be called in four years, so you'd earn closer to five point two, and that's the number I'd count on.

Alright, taxable equivalent yield turns a tax-free muni yield into the pre-tax yield a taxable bond would need to match it. The CFP Board formula is federal only: the tax-exempt yield divided by one minus the marginal rate. Walk it: a three point six percent muni for someone in the thirty-five percent bracket with no state tax is three point six over point six five, about five point five four percent. Now Felix, at thirty-two percent with no state tax, choosing between a six percent corporate and a four point three percent muni. Four point three over point six eight is about six point three two, which beats six, so the muni wins. When the bond is exempt from both federal and state tax, there are two more formulas. For a non-itemizer, divide by one minus both rates added together. For an itemizer, divide by one minus the state rate, times one minus the federal rate, which gives a slightly lower TEY, because paying less state tax also shrinks the state-tax deduction. Grace, who itemizes, with a three point four percent in-state muni at twenty-four federal and six state, gets about four point seven six. As a non-itemizer, about four point eight six. The exam trap: use the state version only when the question gives a state rate and says the bond is exempt from both. To a client: the muni's four point three looks lower, but you keep all of it, and a taxable bond would have to pay about six point three to match.
